board_events.text: From 2D to 3D: adding a third direction
On paper: an origin and two perpendicular axes, x and y, fix any point as an ordered pair.
Lift your pen off the page. That upward direction is a brand-new third axis: z.
Three mutually perpendicular axes meet at one origin O.

board_events.text: The corner of your room is O; its three edges are the x, y, and z axes.
Floor = XY-plane. One wall = YZ-plane. The other wall = ZX-plane.
The three flat surfaces meeting at that corner are the three coordinate planes.
What each coordinate really means
To locate P we ask three questions: how far right, how far in, how far up?
Those three signed numbers are the coordinates (x, y, z).
A coordinate is the signed perpendicular distance of P from a coordinate plane.
Distance from a plane is $|x|$, $|y|$, or $|z|$ — never negative.
The sign only records which side of the plane you are on.
On the floor $z = 0$; on an axis two coordinates are zero; the origin has all three zero.
Eight rooms stacked around the origin
Extend each wall and the floor through the corner: each becomes a full infinite plane.
Three infinite planes cut all of space into eight regions.

board_events.text: Each region is an octant — the 3D cousin of the four quadrants.
Which octant a point sits in is decided entirely by the sign pattern of (x, y, z).
All positive → octant I. All negative → octant VII.
A point with any zero coordinate lies on a boundary and belongs to no octant.

board_events.text: Octants I–IV sit above the floor: $z \gt 0$.
Their (x, y) signs cycle exactly like the four quadrants of the plane.
Octants V–VIII are the mirror images below the floor: $z \lt 0$.
Only octants I (all +) and VII (all −) have a single repeated sign.
To use it: keep only the signs, discard the magnitudes, and read across.
Example: $(-7, 3, -2)$ has pattern $(-,+,-)$ → octant VI.

segments.text: <curious>Ready to leave the flatland you have lived in all through coordinate geometry?</curious> So far every point you have plotted has been trapped on a single sheet of paper. Today we give that world some height.

Think back to how two dimensions work. You fix an origin, draw two perpendicular lines, the x axis and the y axis, and then any point is nailed down by just two numbers, an ordered pair. Clean, but completely flat.
Now do something physical. Lift your pen straight up off the page. That upward direction was never available on the sheet. It is genuinely new and independent, and we call it the z axis.

So now we have three straight lines, each at right angles to the other two, all crossing at a single point. That meeting point is the origin, O. This is the leap from a flat world into the actual room you are sitting in.
Here is the picture. Three axes fanning out from O. Notice each one also runs backwards into its negative half, shown dashed, and the three planes between them are lightly shaded.

Want an anchor you will never forget? Look at the corner of your room where two walls meet the floor. That corner is the origin. The three edges leaving it, one along the floor to your side, one along the floor away from you, one straight up the wall, are your three axes.
And the flat surfaces are the coordinate planes. The floor you would walk on is the X Y plane. One wall is the Y Z plane. The other wall is the Z X plane.
Every wall and the floor is one coordinate plane, and all three slam together exactly at that corner, the origin. Hold this room in your head; the whole chapter lives inside it.
Coordinates are not magic labels; each one answers a very concrete question. Let me make the meaning airtight, because this is exactly the definition examiners test.
To pin down a point P in the room, you ask three things: how far to the right, how far into the room, and how far up. Right, in, up.
Bundle those three answers together, keeping their signs, and you get the ordered triple x, y, z. That is the coordinates of P.
But here is the cleaner, exam-grade way to say what each number is. A coordinate is the signed perpendicular distance of P from a coordinate plane. Perpendicular, and signed.
Precisely: x is the distance from the Y Z plane, y is the distance from the Z X plane, and z is the distance from the X Y plane. Each coordinate is measured against the plane it is not named after.
<whisper>Here is the distinction that trips people up.</whisper> The actual distance from a plane is the absolute value of that coordinate. Distance is never negative, even when the coordinate is.
So what does the sign do? It only records which side of the plane you are standing on. Positive on one side, negative on the other. Same distance, opposite sides.
And watch the special cases. A point resting on the floor has z equal to zero. A point on an axis has two coordinates zero. The origin, sitting at the corner, has all three equal to zero.
We have built one corner of one room. Now let us fill out all of space.
Take each wall and the floor and extend them straight through the corner, out the other side. Each finite surface becomes a full, infinite plane slicing all the way across space.
Three infinite planes, all perpendicular to each other, chop space into pieces. Not four pieces like on paper, but eight.
Picture it: the room you are physically in is one of those eight boxes. Diagonally opposite, on the far side of the origin, sits its mirror-image box.
Each of these eight regions of space is called an octant. It is the direct three-dimensional cousin of the four quadrants you know from the plane.

And the counting is beautiful. Two perpendicular lines gave two squared, four quadrants. Three perpendicular planes give two cubed, which is eight octants. One factor of two per independent direction.
So which octant does a point live in? That is decided entirely by the pattern of signs in its coordinates. The sizes of the numbers are irrelevant; only the plus and minus signs matter.
Anchor on the two easy ones. All three coordinates positive is octant one, the room you are in. All three negative is octant seven, diagonally opposite.
One more crucial thing. If even one coordinate is zero, the point is sitting on a plane or an axis, right on a boundary, and it belongs to no octant at all. Examiners love planting that stray zero.
This little table is, frankly, the single most useful object in the whole subtopic. Learn to read it and half the questions here become instant.
Here it is. Eight columns, one per octant, and three rows for the signs of x, y, and z. Every octant is just a column of three signs.
Read it in two halves. The first four octants, one through four, all sit above the floor, so their z is positive.
And across those four, the x and y signs cycle in exactly the same order as the four quadrants you already know from two-dimensional geometry. Nothing new to memorise there.
The next four, five through eight, are simply the mirror images sitting below the floor, so their z is negative. Same x y dance, one flight of stairs down.
The only two columns that are all one sign are octant one, all positive, and octant seven, all negative. Anchor on those two, then read everything else off the z sign.
To actually use the table on a point, throw away the magnitudes completely. Keep only the sign of each coordinate, then find the matching column.
Take minus seven, three, minus two. Its sign pattern is minus, plus, minus. Scan the table for that column and you land on octant six. Notice the seven and the two did absolutely nothing.

segments.text: kya aap tayaar hain us flatland ko chhodne ke liye jismein aap ab tak coordinate geometry karte aaye hain? ab tak har point ek hi sheet of paper par fansa hua tha. aaj hum us world ko height denge.

yaad karo two dimensions kaise kaam karta hai. ek origin fix karo, do perpendicular lines kheecho, x axis aur y axis, aur phir koi bhi point sirf do numbers se fix ho jata hai, ek ordered pair. saaf, par poori tarah flat.
ab kuch physical karo. apna pen page se seedha upar uthao. wo upward direction sheet par kabhi thi hi nahi. ye bilkul nai aur independent hai, aur ise hum z axis kahte hain.

to ab hamare paas teen straight lines hain, har ek baaki dono ke right angle par, aur teenon ek hi point par milti hain. wo meeting point hai origin, O. yahi hai flat world se us asli room mein chhalang jismein aap baithe ho.
dekho ye picture. teen axes O se baahar nikalti hui. dhyaan do har axis apne negative half mein bhi jaati hai, dashed dikhaya hai, aur beech ke teen planes halke shade kiye hain.

ek aisa anchor chahiye jo kabhi na bhulo? apne room ke us corner ko dekho jahan do walls floor se milti hain. wo corner hai origin. usse nikalti teen edges, ek floor par aapki taraf, ek floor par aapse door, ek seedhi wall ke upar, yahi aapki teen axes hain.
aur wo flat surfaces hain coordinate planes. jis floor par aap chalte, wo hai X Y plane. ek wall hai Y Z plane. doosri wall hai Z X plane.
har wall aur floor ek coordinate plane hai, aur teenon theek usi corner par aakar takrate hain, origin par. is room ko dimaag mein rakho; poora chapter isi ke andar chalta hai.

kisi point P ko room mein fix karne ke liye tum teen cheezen poochhte ho: kitna right, kitna andar, aur kitna upar. Right, in, up.
in teenon jawaboon ko unke signs ke saath mila do, to milta hai ordered triple x, y, z. yahi P ke coordinates hain.
par exam-grade tareeqa ye hai. ek coordinate hai P ki signed perpendicular distance kisi coordinate plane se. Perpendicular, aur signed.
theek-theek: x hai Y Z plane se distance, y hai Z X plane se, aur z hai X Y plane se. Har coordinate us plane se napa jata hai jiske naam par wo nahi hai.
yahin par log phansate hain. kisi plane se asli distance us coordinate ka absolute value hota hai. Distance kabhi negative nahi hota, chahe coordinate negative ho.
to sign kya karta hai? wo sirf batata hai ki tum plane ke kis side par khade ho. ek taraf positive, doosri taraf negative. Distance same, sides opposite.
aur special cases dekho. Floor par baithe point ka z zero hota hai. kisi axis par point ke do coordinates zero. aur origin, corner par, teenon zero.
hamne ek room ka ek corner bana liya. ab poori space bhar dete hain.
har wall aur floor ko corner ke aar-paar kheench do, doosri taraf tak. har finite surface ek poora, infinite plane ban jata hai jo poori space ko kaatata hai.

socho: jis room mein tum ho wo in aath boxes mein se ek hai. theek diagonally opposite, origin ke us paar, uska mirror-image box baitha hai.

segments.text: Almost every exam question on this subtopic is one of three procedures. Let us nail the first two now; reflections get their own section next.
Procedure A, finding the octant, you have basically already seen. Strip each coordinate down to just its sign, then read that triple against the table.
The one thing to internalise: magnitude is a decoy. A coordinate of minus point zero one and a coordinate of minus five hundred are, for octant purposes, identical. Only the sign speaks.
Procedure B is projection, the foot of the perpendicular. To drop a point onto a coordinate plane, you kill exactly one coordinate: the one that plane sets to zero.
Project P onto the X Y plane and the height z simply goes to zero, leaving x, y, zero. The perpendicular runs purely in the z direction, so x and y are untouched.
Same logic elsewhere. Onto the Y Z plane, x dies, giving zero, y, z. Onto the Z X plane, y dies, giving x, zero, z. Each plane erases the one coordinate it is defined by.
The picture makes it vivid. Drop straight down from P to the floor and you lose z first, landing at the foot M. Then slide along to the x-axis and you lose y too, landing at L.
Projecting onto an axis is stricter still. A line is one-dimensional, so only one coordinate survives; you keep the coordinate along that axis and zero the other two.
So the foot on the x-axis is x, zero, zero. On the y-axis, zero, y, zero. On the z-axis, zero, zero, z. Keep one, kill two.
Procedure C is reflection, taking the mirror image of a point. There is one governing idea, and if you hold it, you will never miscount the signs.

The idea: a mirror only reverses the direction that crosses it, and leaves everything within it alone. A plane is two directions wide, so reflecting in it touches only the single perpendicular direction.
Concretely, reflect in the X Y plane and only z flips sign. The point x, y, z becomes x, y, minus z. The x and y live inside the mirror, so they do not move.
By the same rule, reflecting in the Y Z plane flips only x, and reflecting in the Z X plane flips only y. One plane, one sign change, every time.
Now an axis. An axis is only one direction wide, so the two directions perpendicular to it both get reversed. Reflecting in an axis flips two signs.
Reflect in the x-axis and the y and z both flip, while x, lying along the axis, survives. So x, y, z becomes x, minus y, minus z.
And the origin is a point, zero directions wide, so nothing survives. Reflection in the origin reverses all three.
Every coordinate flips: x, y, z becomes minus x, minus y, minus z. It is the same as a full point-inversion through the corner.
So carry one clean rule into the exam. Plane flips one sign, axis flips two, origin flips three. Count the flips first, then apply them. Miscounting is the single commonest error here.
Let us gather every equation from this subtopic into one clean toolkit you can picture on the board.
First the three coordinate planes. Each is defined by setting one coordinate to zero. The X Y plane is z equals zero, the Y Z plane is x equals zero, and the Z X plane is y equals zero.
The three axes need two coordinates zero. The x-axis is y equals zero and z equals zero. The y-axis is x equals zero and z equals zero. The z-axis is x equals zero and y equals zero.
Each coordinate is a signed perpendicular distance. x is the distance of P from the Y Z plane, y from the Z X plane, and z from the X Y plane.
Strip the sign and you get the true distance. The distance from the Y Z plane is the absolute value of x, from the Z X plane the absolute value of y, and from the X Y plane the absolute value of z.
The headcount of regions: two raised to the power three, which is eight octants. One factor of two for each independent sign choice.
And keep the reflection rule in the margin. A plane flips one sign, an axis flips two, the origin flips three.
As the cleanest instance, reflection in the origin sends x, y, z to minus x, minus y, minus z. All three reversed at once.
Let us run a clean CBSE-level example that exercises three separate skills at once: naming an octant, finding a foot of perpendicular, and computing a distance.
The point is P equals five, minus four, nine. Three tasks: which octant is it in, where is its foot on the Z X plane, and how far is it from the X Y plane.
Part a. Ignore the numbers, read the signs. Five is positive, minus four is negative, nine is positive. So the sign pattern is plus, minus, plus.
Scan the octant table for the column plus, minus, plus, and it is octant four. Done, without touching the magnitudes.
Part b, the foot on the Z X plane. First quote the rule: the Z X plane is y equals zero. Projecting onto it kills the y coordinate.
So we set that minus four to zero and leave x and z alone. The foot is five, zero, nine.
Part c, distance from the X Y plane. That plane is z equals zero, so the distance is simply the absolute value of the z coordinate.
The absolute value of nine is nine, so P is nine units from the X Y plane. It is a distance, so there is no sign.
One presentation habit worth marks: always write the rule you are using, like Z X implies y equals zero, before you substitute. In the boards that earns method marks even if your arithmetic slips.

board_events.text: Speed trap: how many lie below the floor?
'Below the XY-plane' just means $z \lt 0$ — octants V–VIII.
So scan only the z-coordinate; ignore x and y entirely.
A: $z=-3$ yes.  B: $z=4$ no.  C: $z=-1$ yes.  D: $z=-2$ yes.
The trap: fully classifying each point wastes a minute.
Read what is actually asked before you compute.
Reflection chain: track the signs in order
$P(4, -3, 7)$: reflect in the YZ-plane to get Q, then reflect Q in the x-axis to get R.
Reflection in the YZ-plane flips only x.
Reflection in the x-axis flips y and z.
Sign pattern of R is $(-, +, -)$.
Order matters: plane = one flip, axis = two flips. Sequence them carefully.
Advanced: locus equidistant from two planes
Find all points equidistant from the XY-plane and the YZ-plane.
Distance from XY is $|z|$; distance from YZ is $|x|$.
So the locus is a PAIR of planes, not one.

board_events.text: Keep the modulus! Solving $x=z$ alone throws away half the locus.
Common pitfalls and the pro-move
Memorise SIGNS, not octant names — the signs are the definition.
Distance of P from a plane is $|x|$, not $x$: for $(-5, 1, 2)$ it is 5, never $-5$.
Any zero coordinate → the point is on a plane or axis, in NO octant.
Examiners plant a stray zero precisely to catch this.
Reflection: plane 1 flip, axis 2, origin 3 — count before you flip.
Pro-move: anchor on octant I (all +) and VII (all −).
Then read the rest off the z-sign: $z \gt 0$ is I–IV, $z \lt 0$ is V–VIII.

segments.text: Now a JEE-Main-style speed trap. Same ideas, but the whole point is to answer fast and not fall into busywork.
We are given four points: A, B, C, and D, with the coordinates on the board. The question asks how many of them lie in octants that are entirely below the X Y plane.
Translate the words first. Entirely below the X Y plane means the z coordinate is negative. Those are octants five through eight. The question is really only about the sign of z.
So do not classify anything. Just run your eye down the z coordinates and count the negatives. x and y are pure distraction here.
A has z equals minus three, negative, yes. B has z equals four, positive, no. C has z equals minus one, yes. D has z equals minus two, yes.
Three of the four have negative z. So the answer is three. That took about ten seconds.
Here is the trap the question is built around. A rushed student starts fully naming octant five, octant two, and so on for each point, and burns a full minute.
The fix is a habit: read exactly what is being asked before you compute. The question touched only one coordinate's sign, so you only needed one coordinate.
This one chains two reflections together, so it tests whether you know that a plane and an axis flip different numbers of signs, and whether you can keep the order straight.
Start with P equals four, minus three, seven. First we reflect it in the Y Z plane to get a point Q, then we reflect Q in the x-axis to get R, and we want R's octant.
First reflection, in the Y Z plane. A plane flips exactly one sign, the perpendicular one. The Y Z plane is perpendicular to the x direction, so only x changes sign.
So four becomes minus four, and y and z ride along unchanged. Q is minus four, minus three, seven.
Second reflection, now in the x-axis. An axis flips two signs, the two perpendicular to it. For the x-axis those are y and z.
Starting from Q, we flip its y and z. Minus three becomes plus three, seven becomes minus seven, and the x stays minus four. So R is minus four, three, minus seven.
Now read R's signs. Minus four is negative, three is positive, minus seven is negative. Pattern minus, plus, minus.
That column in the table is octant six. So R lands in octant six.
The lesson is discipline. Reflection in a plane is one flip, in an axis is two, and doing them in the wrong order, or flipping the wrong count, drops you in a completely different octant.
Let us finish the subtopic with a JEE Advanced flavour, where the whole game is rigour, specifically not losing half the answer.
The task: find every point in space that is equidistant from the X Y plane and the Y Z plane. Set up, do not guess.
Recall the distances. A point's distance from the X Y plane is the absolute value of z. Its distance from the Y Z plane is the absolute value of x. Equidistant means those two are equal.
So the condition is absolute value of x equals absolute value of z. And this is the exact moment students get careless.
Square both sides to remove the moduli: x squared equals z squared, so x squared minus z squared is zero, which factors into x minus z, times x plus z, equals zero.
A product is zero when either factor is zero. So this is not one surface, it is a pair of planes.
The two planes are x equals z, and x equals minus z. And notice y never appeared in the condition, so y is completely free; each of these is a full plane containing the entire y-axis.
If you look straight down the y-axis, the two planes appear edge-on as two lines crossing at the origin, an X-shape. They are the planes that bisect the angle between the X Y and Y Z planes.

And here is the rigour lesson worth real marks. The modulus is non-negotiable. If you dropped it and solved only x equals z, you would silently throw away the second plane, the classic Advanced deduction.
Let us close Subtopic one by collecting the mistakes that quietly cost marks, and the one habit that makes you fast.

First pitfall: trying to memorise octant names like some Roman-numeral chant. That is fragile. The signs are the actual definition; the numeral is just a label hanging off them. Learn the sign table, not the names.

Second: confusing a coordinate with a distance. The distance of a point from a plane is the absolute value of the coordinate, never the raw signed value. For minus five, one, two, the distance from the Y Z plane is five, not minus five. Distances are never negative.
Third, and the most planted trap: if any coordinate is zero, the point is sitting on a plane or an axis, and it belongs to no octant whatsoever.
Examiners slip a zero into a coordinate on purpose, hoping you will force it into some octant anyway. Spot the zero and state that it is on a boundary.
Fourth: reflection sign errors. Keep the count in your margin. A plane flips one sign, an axis flips two, the origin flips three. Count first, then flip.
Now the pro-move that ties it together. Anchor on the only two clean octants: octant one is all positive, octant seven is all negative.

From there, read everything off the z sign. Positive z lands you in octants one through four, behaving just like the plane's quadrants; negative z drops you into five through eight, the same quadrant pattern mirrored below the floor.

board_events.text: Distance in 3D: Pythagoras, applied twice
On paper, the gap is $\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}$ — a right-triangle hypotenuse.

segments.text: We can name points in space now. This subtopic is about measuring with them, and the first tool is distance. <curious>The good news?</curious> You already know the hard part.

On flat paper, the distance between two points is the square root of delta x squared plus delta y squared. That is nothing but the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the horizontal and vertical gaps.
Space just adds one more perpendicular direction, the z direction. So we do not learn a new idea; we apply Pythagoras a second time, stacked on the first.
Picture a drone hovering in a room. Here is the box it sits in, with the two corner points at opposite ends of the space diagonal.
To reach the drone from the corner, first walk across the floor to the spot directly beneath it, that is an ordinary two-dimensional distance, then rise straight up by delta z.

So the true straight-line distance is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose two legs are the floor distance and the height. Squaring: distance squared equals delta x squared plus delta y squared, the floor leg, plus delta z squared, the height leg.
Collapse those two Pythagoras steps into one and you have written the entire three-dimensional distance formula. No memorisation, just the picture.
And this is exactly why the longest rod you can fit into a room lies along the space-diagonal of the box. Same triangle, read the other way.
The second tool is the section formula: given two points and a ratio, find the point that splits the segment between them. It looks like it should be messy in three dimensions. It is not.
Set the scene. A point R sits on the segment from P to Q and divides it in some given ratio, and we want R's coordinates, all three of them.
Here is the secret that makes it easy. Each coordinate is really just a projection of the point onto an axis, and a fundamental fact of parallel projection is that it preserves ratios.
So a single division happening in three-dimensional space quietly becomes three separate, identical one-dimensional divisions, one along each axis. You solve the same little problem three times.

Think of a toll booth on the Mumbai to Pune expressway dividing the route two to three. Then its easting, its northing, and its altitude are each the same two-to-three split of the endpoints. One ratio, three coordinates.

Now the two flavours. If R lies between P and Q, the division is internal, like a booth on the road. If R lies on the line through P and Q but outside the segment, beyond either end, it is external, an extrapolation.

The only real difference shows up in the arithmetic. Internally the two parts of the ratio add in the denominator; externally they subtract. That single plus-versus-minus is the entire gap between the two formulas.

And one clean unification: a negative ratio is just external division wearing a disguise. Dividing in m to n externally is the same as dividing in m to minus n internally. Watch the signs, not the words.
Before we list formulas, let us lock down the edge cases. These are exactly where the questions are designed to trip you.
First, an assumption baked into the section formula: it only ever produces a point on the line through P and Q. It divides that line; it cannot give you a point floating off to the side.
The midpoint is not a separate formula to memorise. It is just the section formula with the ratio one to one, internal. Averaging the coordinates falls straight out of that.
Now a genuine breakdown. External division is undefined when m equals n, because the external denominator is m minus n, and that becomes zero. Division by zero, no answer.

And the geometry agrees with the algebra. Equal external parts push the dividing point infinitely far away, off to infinity, the way two parallel lines never meet. So the formula rightly refuses to give a finite point.
Remember the disguise from a moment ago: a negative ratio, m to minus n, is exactly external division written another way. If a problem hands you a negative k, read it as external.
Finally, distance. Distance is always greater than or equal to zero. That is true even though the coordinate differences inside the formula, delta x, delta y, delta z, can each be negative.
The reason is the squaring. Every difference gets squared, which erases its sign, so the direction you measure in never changes the distance. Going from P to Q or Q to P gives the same number.
Here is the complete formula toolkit for this subtopic, all on one board. Learn the shapes, not just the symbols.
The distance between P and Q is the square root of the sum of the three squared coordinate differences. Delta x squared, plus delta y squared, plus delta z squared, all under one root.
Distance from the origin is the same formula with P at the origin, so it is just the square root of x squared plus y squared plus z squared. The length of the position, effectively.
Internal section in ratio m to n. Each coordinate is m times the far point plus n times the near point, over m plus n. Same recipe for x, y, and z; only the coordinate changes.
External section is the twin with two sign changes: minus in each numerator and m minus n in the denominator. Internal adds, external subtracts. Hold those side by side.
The midpoint is the friendly special case: just average each pair of coordinates. It is internal one to one, and the m plus n becomes two.
The workhorse is the k to one form. Set the ratio as k to one and a general point on the line is k times the far point plus the near point, over k plus one. One unknown does everything.
The centroid of a triangle is the plain average of its three vertices, each coordinate summed and divided by three. Balance point of the triangle, coordinate by coordinate.

Two flags to keep. In the k to one form, a positive k means internal and a negative k means external, so the sign hands you the case for free. And a tetrahedron's centroid is the same average of its four vertices, divided by four instead of three.

board_events.text: Worked example: classify the triangle
Show $A(0,7,10)$, $B(-1,6,6)$, $C(-4,9,6)$ form a right-angled isosceles triangle.
$AB^2=BC^2$ → two sides equal → isosceles.
Converse of Pythagoras → right angle at B.
Work with squared lengths; take roots only if asked.
Speed trap: ratio at which a plane cuts a segment
In what ratio does the XY-plane divide the join of $P(2,-3,5)$ and $Q(4,6,-10)$?
XY-plane is $z = 0$ — force only the z-coordinate to zero.
$k \gt 0$ → internal; ratio $k:1 = 1:2$.
The sign of k already tells you internal vs external — no separate check.
Ignore x and y entirely: for a plane $z = 0$, only the z-equation matters.
Worked example: equidistant point on the y-axis
Find the point on the y-axis equidistant from $A(3,1,2)$ and $B(-1,5,-4)$.
A point on the y-axis has the form $R(0, y, 0)$ — three unknowns collapse to one.
Impose $RA^2 = RB^2$.
The point is $\left(0,\ \tfrac{7}{2},\ 0\right)$.
The $y^2$ terms cancel — an 'equidistant' condition is always linear.
Advanced: locus equidistant from two points
Find all points equidistant from $A(1,2,3)$ and $B(3,2,-1)$; describe the surface.
Take $P(x,y,z)$ with $PA^2 = PB^2$.

sections.title: Common pitfalls and the k:1 pro-move & related topics

board_events.text: Pitfalls and the k:1 pro-move
INT ⇒ add ($m+n$); EXT ⇒ subtract ($m-n$). Do not mix them.
Ratio order: $m:n$ means $PR:RQ$, so $m$ pairs with the far point $x_2$.
Reversing which point is P silently inverts your ratio (the $3:5$ vs $5:3$ trap).
Square the coordinate differences, and root the sum at the end — skip neither.
Three points may be collinear — always test before claiming a triangle.
Pro-move: for any 'find the ratio' question, jump straight to the $k:1$ form.
One unknown, and the sign of $k$ gives internal ($k \gt 0$) vs external ($k \lt 0$) free.
The centroid: where a triangle balances
Cut a triangle from card; the point where it balances on a fingertip is the centroid G.

board_events.text: G is where the three medians meet.
Each median is split by G in the ratio $2:1$, measured from the vertex.
In coordinates, G is simply the average of the three vertices.
It is an average because each coordinate balances independently — three 1D acts.
The centroid always exists and is unique; it does not depend on side lengths.
Collinearity: three points, one line
Three points are collinear when they lie on one line — they fail to make a triangle.
Distance lens: if B lies between A and C, then $AB + BC = AC$.
Section lens: B divides AC in $k:1$ — the SAME k for x, y, and z.
Three roadside milestones: the middle splits the outer two by one fixed proportion.
If even one of the three coordinate proportions disagrees, the point is off the line.
Collinear points make the triangle's area zero — a useful sanity flag.
So collinearity is a statement about all three coordinates locking to one ratio.

segments.text: Let us close Subtopic two with the errors that quietly cost marks and the one move that makes ratio questions trivial.

First and commonest: mixing up internal and external. Internal uses m plus n in the denominator with a plus in the numerator; external uses m minus n with a minus. Write INT adds, EXT subtracts in your margin before you substitute.
Second, ratio order. m to n means P R to R Q, so m is the part next to Q and it pairs with the far point, x two, in the numerator. Keep that pairing fixed.

If you quietly swap which point you called P and which you called Q, your ratio flips. That is the classic three to five versus five to three mistake, and it turns a correct method into a wrong answer.
Third, the mechanical slips. You must square each coordinate difference inside the formula, and you must root the whole sum at the very end. Skip either step and the answer is simply wrong.

Fourth, do not assume three given points make a triangle. They might be collinear. Always test first, with the distance sum, the section ratio, or by checking a midpoint, before you start calling it a triangle.
Now the pro-move that ties the ratio work together. For any question that asks for a ratio, or where a plane cuts a segment, go straight to the k to one form.

It uses a single unknown instead of two, and the sign of k hands you the case for free: positive k is internal, negative k is external. No separate case analysis, and you get the dividing ratio as a bonus.
Subtopic three is where the two tools we just built, distance and the section formula, start earning marks. We open with the centroid.
Here is the physical meaning. Cut a triangle out of stiff card and balance it on a single fingertip. There is exactly one point where it sits level, and that point is the centroid, written G.
Geometrically, the centroid is where the three medians of the triangle meet, as shown. A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
All three medians pass through the one point G. That concurrency is not an accident; it falls out of the coordinate formula we will derive shortly.
And G sits at a very specific spot on each median. It divides every median in the ratio two to one, measured from the vertex, so it is twice as far from the vertex as from the opposite side.
Now the payoff in coordinates, and it is beautifully simple. The centroid is just the average of the three vertices. Add the x coordinates and divide by three, and likewise for y and z.

Why an average and not something messier? Because, as always in this chapter, each coordinate behaves on its own. Balancing in three dimensions is really three separate one-dimensional balancing acts, one per axis.

One clean fact to bank: the centroid always exists and is always unique, and it depends only on the vertices, not on the side lengths. That last point will matter when we meet the incentre, which does weight by side lengths.
Next application: collinearity, the test for whether three points sit on a single straight line.
Three points are collinear when they all lie on one line, which is the same as saying they fail to form a triangle, the triangle has collapsed flat.
There are two honest ways to detect it. The distance lens: if the point B lies between A and C, then the long hop equals the sum of the two short hops. A B plus B C equals A C.

The section lens, which is what JEE rewards: if the points are collinear, then B must divide A C in some real ratio, k to one, and crucially the same k has to work for the x, the y, and the z coordinates all at once.

Picture three milestones along the expressway. If they are truly on the road, the middle one splits the distance between the outer two in one fixed proportion, and that same proportion holds whether you measure easting, northing, or altitude.
But if even one of those three proportions disagrees, the middle milestone is off the road. There is no single straight line through all three.
A handy sanity flag: collinear points make the triangle's area exactly zero. If you ever compute a nonzero area, they were not collinear.
So hold the real meaning. Collinearity is not about one coordinate; it is a statement that all three coordinates lock onto one and the same ratio. Checking only x is the classic false positive.

board_events.text: Locus: shaping surfaces from a rule
A locus is all points obeying a condition; in 3D, distance rules carve surfaces.
Equidistant from two fixed points → a flat plane (the perpendicular bisector).
At a fixed distance from one fixed point → a sphere.

board_events.text: Like every spot a tethered goat can graze around its peg.
Sum of distances from two points constant → an ellipsoid (the 3D ellipse).
Two points → plane; one point → sphere; constant sum → ellipsoid.
When these applications degenerate
Centroid: always exists, always unique; unlike the incentre, ignores side lengths.
Collinearity makes the triangle's area zero — a degenerate 'triangle'.
A sphere is real only if its radius-squared is positive.
Radius-squared zero → a single point; negative → the empty set.
The ellipsoid is real only if the constant sum exceeds the distance between the points.
You cannot beat the straight line: the shortest path is the segment itself.
Reading these limits stops you 'finding' a surface that does not exist.
Testing collinearity: two methods
Method A (distance): collinear iff the largest of AB, BC, CA equals the other two's sum.
If $AB + BC = AC$, then B lies between A and C.
Method B (section-ratio): let B divide AC in $k:1$; solve k from the x-coordinate alone.
Then VERIFY the same k reproduces $y_2$ and $z_2$.

All three agree → collinear, and you get the dividing ratio for free.

segments.text: The third application is locus, and it is where three-dimensional geometry gets genuinely three-dimensional, because distance conditions now carve out whole surfaces.
A locus is simply the set of all points that obey a stated condition. On paper such conditions gave curves; in space they give surfaces. Two of them carry this chapter.

First, equidistant from two fixed points. Every such point is equally far from A and from B, and together they form a flat plane, the perpendicular bisector plane, exactly the one we derived in Subtopic two.
Second, at a fixed distance from one fixed point. Every point exactly r away from a centre forms a sphere.
Here it is: a sphere of radius r centred at C. Every point on the surface is the same distance r from the centre, in every direction.
The homely picture is a goat tied to a peg by a rope. The set of all spots it can just reach traces out a sphere, of radius equal to the rope.
And a richer condition: the sum of the distances from two fixed points is held constant. That bends space into an ellipsoid, the three-dimensional cousin of the ellipse you know from the plane.
So carry the family in your head. Equidistant from two points gives a plane. Fixed distance from one point gives a sphere. A constant sum of two distances gives an ellipsoid.
Before the formulas, a quick tour of the edge cases, because these applications each have a way of degenerating that examiners like to probe.

The centroid is the well-behaved one. It always exists and is always unique, and it depends only on the vertices. Contrast that with the incentre, which weights the vertices by side lengths and so does care about shape.
Collinearity is really the degenerate case of a triangle: the three points line up and the enclosed area drops to zero. It is a triangle only in name.
For a sphere written in expanded form, reality has a condition. It is a genuine sphere only if the computed radius-squared comes out positive.

If that radius-squared is exactly zero, the locus shrinks to a single point. If it is negative, there are no real points at all, the locus is the empty set. Always check the sign before declaring a sphere.
The ellipsoid has its own reality check. The sum-of-distances ellipsoid exists only if the constant sum is strictly larger than the distance between the two fixed points.

The reason is simple geometry: you cannot beat the straight line. The shortest possible sum of distances to the two points is the straight segment joining them, so a smaller target sum has no solutions.
Reading these limits is not pedantry. It is what stops you from confidently finding a surface in an exam that, in fact, does not exist.
There are two clean procedures for testing collinearity. Method A is intuitive; Method B is faster and is what JEE actually rewards.
Method A uses distances. Compute all three pairwise distances, A B, B C, and C A. The points are collinear if and only if the largest of the three equals the sum of the other two.
Concretely, if A B plus B C equals A C, then B sits between A and C on the line. No slack means no bend.
Method B uses the section ratio and is usually quicker. Suppose B divides A C in the ratio k to one, and solve for k using just the x coordinate.
So set k x three plus x one, over k plus one, equal to x two, and solve. That gives a candidate value of k from one equation.
Now the step that is not optional: verify that the very same k also reproduces y two and z two. Plug it back into the y and the z equations.

Why is verification non-negotiable? Because a single coordinate can match by pure coincidence. Solving from x and stopping is the classic false positive that turns a non-collinear trio into a wrong yes.
If all three coordinates agree on that one k, the points are genuinely collinear, and as a bonus you already hold the ratio in which B divides A C.

segments.text: Here is the applications toolkit, gathering every formula from this subtopic, including the two JEE extensions.
The centroid of a triangle is the plain average of its three vertices. Sum each coordinate, divide by three. That is the single most-used formula here.
Collinearity as a formula: the points are collinear exactly when B divides A C in a ratio k to one that solves the x equation and reproduces y and z with the same k. One ratio, all three coordinates.
The sphere: all points at distance r from a centre a, b, c satisfy x minus a squared plus y minus b squared plus z minus c squared equals r squared. Memorise the shape, not the letters.
The perpendicular bisector: the set of points equidistant from A and B, where P A equals P B, is a plane. Linear condition, flat surface.
The ellipsoid: a constant sum of distances equal to two a, with the relation b squared equals a squared minus c squared linking the semi-axes to the half-distance between foci. The spatial ellipse.
And the first JEE extension, the incentre. Unlike the centroid, it is a weighted average, each vertex weighted by the length of the opposite side, a, b, and c, over the perimeter a plus b plus c.

Hold the contrast in one line. The centroid is a plain average; the incentre is a weighted average. And the second extension: a tetrahedron's centroid is the average of its four vertices, dividing by four.
A two-part centroid example, forward and then in reverse, because the reverse version is a favourite and has one classic slip.
Part a is the straightforward direction. Given the three vertices A, B, and C, find the centroid.

Just average each coordinate. The x average is two plus six plus one over three, which is three. The y average is minus one plus three plus four over three, which is two. The z average is four minus two plus five over three, which is seven thirds. So G is three, two, seven thirds.
Part b runs it backwards. Now we are told two of the vertices and the centroid, three, two, seven thirds, and we must recover the missing third vertex.
Use the definition in reverse. Since the centroid is the average, the sum of all three vertices equals three times the centroid. So multiply the centroid through by three.

Solve coordinate by coordinate. For x, three times three is nine, minus the two known x values, two and six, leaves one. For y, three times two is six, minus minus one, minus three, gives four. For z, three times seven thirds is seven, minus four, minus minus two, gives five.
So the third vertex is one, four, five, which is reassuringly the same C we started with in part a. The forward and reverse are consistent.

The one thing that trips students on the reverse problem: the sum of the vertices is three times the centroid, not the centroid itself. Forget that factor of three and every coordinate comes out wrong.
A JEE-Main speed trap on collinearity. The trap is entirely about the verification step, so watch it closely.
The question: are the three points A, B, and C collinear? Coordinates are on the board.
Use Method B. Suppose B divides A C in the ratio k to one, and solve for k from the x coordinate alone, to get a candidate quickly.
The x equation is eight k plus two, over k plus one, equals four. Clear the denominator: eight k plus two equals four k plus four, so four k equals two, and k is one half.
Now the step you must not skip: check that this k, one half, also works for y and for z. This is where careless students have already declared victory and lost the marks.

For y: ten times one half plus one, over three halves, is six over three halves, which is four, matching B's y. For z: eleven times one half minus one, over three halves, is three and a half over one and a half, which is three, matching B's z. Both check out.
All three coordinates agree on k equals one half, so the points are genuinely collinear, and B divides A C in the ratio one to two.

Here is the whole point of the trap. If the y check or the z check had disagreed, the answer would flip completely to not collinear. A clean k from x alone proves nothing; one coordinate is never proof.

board_events.text: Worked example: parallelogram or rectangle?
Show $A(1,0,2)$, $B(4,2,3)$, $C(5,7,2)$, $D(2,5,1)$ form a parallelogram ABCD.
Opposite sides equal and parallel → ABCD is a parallelogram.
Rectangle test: are the diagonals equal?
$65 \ne 17$ → diagonals unequal → NOT a rectangle.
Equivalently $\vec{AB}\cdot\vec{AD}=12\ne 0$: adjacent sides not perpendicular.
Advanced: locus of constant distance-sum
Find the locus of P with $PA+PB=12$, where $A(5,0,0)$, $B(-5,0,0)$.
Isolate one radical and square — then isolate and square again.

board_events.text: Kill the double radical in TWO squaring rounds — one root isolated each time.
Application pitfalls and pro-moves
Declaring collinearity from one coordinate is the top error — confirm k across y and z.
Centroid ÷3 (triangle) or ÷4 (tetrahedron); midpoint ÷2; incentre = weighted.
Reverse centroid: 'sum of vertices $= 3G$', not $G$ — keep the ×3.
Two POINTS equidistant is linear (plane); ONE point distance is quadratic (sphere).
For sum-of-distances, isolate and square one radical at a time.
Figure type: all sides equal = rhombus; equal diagonals = rectangle; both = square.
Pro-move: 'collinear / what ratio' → solve k from one coordinate, verify the other two.

segments.text: This example classifies a quadrilateral, first proving it is a parallelogram, then testing whether it is a rectangle. The cleanest route is side vectors.
We are given four points A, B, C, D, in order, and must show A B C D is a parallelogram.

A quadrilateral is a parallelogram when both pairs of opposite sides are equal and parallel, which for vectors just means the side vectors are equal. Compute A B as three, two, one; and D C, that is C minus D, also three, two, one. So A B equals D C.
Do the other pair. A D is one, five, minus one; and B C, that is C minus B, is also one, five, minus one. So A D equals B C.
Both pairs of opposite sides are equal and parallel, so A B C D is a parallelogram. That is the first claim settled.
Now, is it a rectangle? A parallelogram is a rectangle exactly when its two diagonals are equal in length, so we compare the squared diagonals A C and B D.
A C squared is four squared plus seven squared plus zero, which is sixty-five. B D squared is minus two squared plus three squared plus minus two squared, which is seventeen.
Sixty-five is not seventeen, so the diagonals have different lengths, and therefore the parallelogram is not a rectangle.

You can confirm it another way: the dot product of A B with A D is three plus ten minus one, which is twelve, not zero. Nonzero dot product means the adjacent sides are not perpendicular, again ruling out a rectangle.
We finish the chapter's teaching with a JEE Advanced classic: a locus defined by a constant sum of distances. The whole discipline here is handling two square roots without wrecking the algebra.
The condition is that the point P keeps its distance to A plus its distance to B fixed at twelve, with A and B given on the x-axis at plus and minus five.

Write it out. The square root of x minus five squared plus y squared plus z squared, plus the square root of x plus five squared plus y squared plus z squared, equals twelve. Two radicals in one equation.

You cannot square that in one shot; you would just create a new cross term with a radical still in it. Instead, isolate one radical on its own side, square, then isolate the remaining radical and square a second time.

After the first isolate-and-square, the common x squared plus y squared plus z squared plus twenty-five terms cancel, and tidying leaves twenty-four times the square root of x plus five squared plus y squared plus z squared equals one hundred forty-four plus twenty x.
Divide by four and square the second time. That gives thirty-six times the bracket x plus five squared plus y squared plus z squared equals thirty-six plus five x, all squared.

segments.text: Let us actually derive the distance formula the way the boards want it, using a rectangular box. Once you see the two right triangles hiding inside, it is unforgettable.

Setup. Through P and through Q, draw planes parallel to the three coordinate planes. Those six planes box in a rectangular parallelepiped, and P and Q are the two ends of its space diagonal, with every edge parallel to an axis.
Here is the box with the key points marked. A is the vertex at P's height sitting directly below Q, and N is the vertex that completes the floor triangle from P.
First, split off the height. The edge A to Q runs purely vertically, along z, while P to A lies flat in a horizontal plane, so they meet at a right angle. Triangle P A Q is right-angled at A.
Pythagoras there gives P Q squared equals P A squared plus A Q squared. That peels the vertical part away from the horizontal part.
Now resolve that horizontal leg P A. It sits in a flat plane and is itself the hypotenuse of a right triangle P N A, with legs running along the x and y directions and the right angle at N.
So P A squared equals P N squared plus N A squared. We have now broken the whole diagonal into three axis-aligned pieces.

And because every edge is parallel to an axis, each length is just the gap in that coordinate. P N is the absolute value of x two minus x one, N A the absolute value of y two minus y one, and A Q the absolute value of z two minus z one.

Substitute the second equation into the first, and the squares wipe out the absolute values. P Q equals the square root of delta x squared plus delta y squared plus delta z squared. That is the distance formula, fully earned.
Now the section formula. The whole derivation rides on one idea we already met: parallel projection preserves ratios. Let us make it concrete for the z coordinate, then get the others for free.
Setup. Let R divide the segment P Q internally, so the ratio P R to R Q is m to n. We want R's coordinates.
Here is the picture. Three parallel perpendiculars drop from P, R, and Q straight down to the X Y plane, landing at L, N, and M.
Because all three perpendiculars are parallel, dropping to the same plane, they carry the division faithfully. Whatever ratio R makes on the top line, its shadow N makes on the bottom line.
That is the key fact stated plainly. If R divides P Q in m to n, then N divides L M in the same m to n. Projection does not distort the ratio.
Track the heights, the z coordinates, through similar triangles. The ratio P R to R Q equals z minus z one, over z two minus z, and that equals m over n.
Cross-multiply: n times z minus z one equals m times z two minus z. Collect the z terms and you get z equals m z two plus n z one, all over m plus n.
Now the payoff. Run the identical construction projecting onto the Y Z plane and the Z X plane, and by pure symmetry you get x and y in exactly the same shape. Three coordinates, one derivation.
And external division needs no new work. Just replace n by minus n throughout, and the denominator turns from m plus n into m minus n. That is where the external formula's minus signs come from.
Let us derive the centroid formula, and notice it needs nothing new: it is the section formula plus one known property of triangles.
Set up the triangle A, B, C and take the median from vertex A to the point D, the midpoint of the opposite side B C.
By the midpoint formula from Subtopic two, D is the average of B and C: each coordinate is B's plus C's, over two.

Now use the one property we borrow from geometry: the centroid divides every median in the ratio two to one from the vertex. So G divides the segment A D internally with A G to G D equal to two to one.

Apply the internal section formula with ratio two to one, A as first point, D as second. For the x coordinate: two times D's x, plus one times A's x, over two plus one. The two cancels the halves inside D, and it collapses to x one plus x two plus x three, over three.
Run the identical algebra for the y and z coordinates. Nothing changes but the letter.
So the centroid is the plain average of all three vertices, coordinate by coordinate. Sum and divide by three.

And here is a bonus. If you had instead started from the median out of B, or out of C, you would land on exactly the same point G. That is a clean proof that all three medians are concurrent, they genuinely meet at one point.
Here is your complete toolkit for Chapter eleven, everything on one board. This is a recap, so I will restate each item, not re-derive it.
From Subtopic one: the three coordinate planes are z equals zero, x equals zero, and y equals zero, and three perpendicular planes cut space into two cubed, eight octants.
The distance between two points is the square root of the summed squared coordinate differences. Your most-used single formula.
Internal section in m to n: each coordinate is m times the far point plus n times the near point, over m plus n.
External section is the same with m minus n denominators and minus signs; and the midpoint is just the one-to-one case, the average of the endpoints.
The triangle centroid is the plain average of its three vertices; for a tetrahedron, average four and divide by four.
The sphere: points at distance r from a centre a, b, c, in the standard squared form equal to r squared.
And the ellipsoid from a constant sum of distances, with b squared equals a squared minus c squared linking its axes to the foci.

Two quick reminders in the margin. Reflections flip one sign for a plane, two for an axis, three for the origin. And for locus: equidistant from two points is a plane, a fixed distance from one point is a sphere.
Finally, the one-screen cheat sheet for the whole chapter, the things to glance at the night before the exam.
The frame: three axes, three planes, eight octants. The plane equations are z equals zero, x equals zero, and y equals zero.
Each coordinate is a signed perpendicular distance from a plane, and the actual distance from a plane is the absolute value of that coordinate.
Keep the octant sign table in view; it answers every octant question in one glance.
Reflections by flip count: a plane flips one sign, an axis two, the origin three.
The distance formula is the root of the summed squared differences. For section problems, internal adds and external subtracts, and the k to one form handles every ratio question.
The centroid is a plain average, dividing by three for a triangle or four for a tetrahedron, while the incentre is a weighted average by side lengths.
Collinear means one ratio k to one fits x, y, and z together, or equivalently A B plus B C equals A C.

And the locus family: equidistant from two points gives a plane, a fixed distance from one point gives a sphere, and a constant sum of two distances gives an ellipsoid. That is the whole chapter on one card.
